title: The hidden cost of the quick question
performance: before sending or answering the next non-urgent question, the viewer can tell whether it needs an answer now or can wait for a batch, and can propose to their team two or three habits that move when questions land: batching non-urgent questions, agreed focus time with an urgent route, and a short ready-to-resume note before switching

audience.assumed_prior: works on chat and email all day; knows from experience that a morning of small messages can leave real work unfinished; has probably heard that multitasking is bad and maybe a recovery-time figure; no model of why a one-minute answer costs more than a minute
audience.why: the brief's audience is knowledge workers and managers already doing the job (practitioners), novices in the mechanism; the knowledge sheet defines each term (F1, F4, F6) and assumes nothing but office work
audience.motivation: probably assigned or browsing a course, not stated; they care about their own deep work and about not becoming the colleague who never answers, so relevance must land in the first seconds and nothing may sound like a lecture about being distracted
audience.context: not stated; plan for a desk or laptop with sound and captions on (the project requests captions), first-language English assumed but not confirmed, so screens carry short anchors and nothing rests on audio alone

strategy.name: concrete_first
strategy.rationale: the knowledge sheet is a chain of mechanisms (switch cost F1, resumption lag F4, attention residue F6, errors after brief interruptions F5) that are abstract as names but obvious in one case: a single question arriving in the middle of one piece of work; the brief asks for the cost shown on that one morning, so the case comes first and each name is attached to something the viewer has just watched happen
strategy.signature_move: show the moment on the one morning, put what it costs on the two-column ledger (visible, hidden), THEN name the idea just shown

misconceptions.belief: a quick question costs about the minute it takes to answer
misconceptions.why_tempting: the minute is the only part anyone sees; the answer is short and the asker is grateful
misconceptions.source_anchor: knowledge F1, F4, F6, F5; brief through_line
misconceptions.refutation: the visible column holds one small unit for the answer; then the hidden column fills as the work is swapped back in (switch, finding your place, part of your attention still on the question); the minute was the smallest thing on the ledger

misconceptions.belief: I can keep writing and answer messages at the same time, so for me there is no switch
misconceptions.why_tempting: it feels like doing both at once, and the work does keep moving
misconceptions.source_anchor: knowledge F3; not_claimed (natural multitaskers who pay no switching cost)
misconceptions.refutation: one line only: for two tasks that both need attention, what feels like doing both is switching back and forth, and each switch goes on the ledger (F3); the slot visibly swaps rather than holding two things

misconceptions.belief: if I just answer fast and catch up, the cost disappears
misconceptions.why_tempting: people do speed up after interruptions and the work still gets done
misconceptions.refutation: in one experiment people did speed up, but reported more stress and effort (F8, caveated as one lab study); the hidden column does not empty, its units change label from time to strain

misconceptions.belief: the fix is to ask fewer questions, or to stop answering them
misconceptions.why_tempting: if questions cause the cost, fewer questions seems the obvious cure
misconceptions.refutation: questions unblock work (F17, F11: the asker really does get unstuck); the habits keep every question and change only when non-urgent ones land, so the visible column stays the same while the hidden column shrinks

running_example.framing: clearly invented, introduced with 'say' in the hook; second person: YOU are the one deep in the work in sec1, and in sec2 the viewer is flipped into the asker's seat; no names, no real company, no named chat or email product
running_example.piece_of_work: one focused piece of work held through the morning, say a plan or a report you are writing
invented_details: the questions are plausible one-liners from colleagues (say, where is the latest version, can you check this figure), each answerable in about a minute
a handful of such questions across one morning; the count is illustrative and framed as 'say'
any size for the hidden part is framed as hypothetical ('say it takes a few minutes to get back in') and immediately caveated that the real figure varies (F18)
running_example.rule: one worker, one piece of work, one morning; no second scenario; no recovery figure stated as fact; no statistics; the same morning returns at the payoff

hook.sketch: Say you are deep in a plan and a message lands: quick question? It takes a minute to answer. So why, by lunch, does the plan look exactly as you left it?
hook.on_screen_essence: Quick question? One minute. So where did the morning go?

arc.promise: in the next two minutes, where the rest of that cost goes, and two or three habits a team can use to stop paying it without asking fewer questions
arc.bridge_from_prior: sec1 opens from the feeling every viewer has had: a morning of small messages and an untouched piece of real work

sections.title: The minute you see, and the part you do not
sections.goal: the viewer can explain why answering one quick question costs more than the minute it takes: the switch, finding your place again, and attention left behind
sections.carrier: one piece of work held in a slot on the page; the question swaps it out and back while a two-column ledger (visible, hidden) fills unit by unit as each part is named: one small visible unit for the answer, then the hidden column grows with the switch, the search for your place, and a faint unit of attention still on the question
sections.recap: the answer is the visible part; switching away and getting back in is the hidden part
sections.teaching_notes: worked example of ONE question, traced completely with the signature move; three new terms, each named only after the viewer has seen it happen; F5 in one line as an experiment (even a few seconds' interruption made people lose their place in a step-by-step task), caveated as a lab finding; refute misconception 1 by the ledger itself, and misconception 2 in one line (F3); slowdown here on the hidden part; no magnitude is stated as fact

sections.title: A morning of quick questions
sections.goal: the viewer can use the visible and hidden split to show where a morning of quick questions really goes, and on whom the cost lands
concepts: the asker gets unstuck, the cost lands on the interrupted
sections.carrier: the same morning as a grid of time units: each of a handful of questions stamps one visible unit and a larger run of hidden units (sizes framed as hypothetical), so the hidden pile visibly outgrows the visible one; the units that the worker races through relabel from time to strain; then the frame flips to the asker's side, where the same question is one small, useful unit
sections.teaching_notes: the viewer applies sec1's split to a whole morning, question by question, faster each time (faded: the narrator stops naming the parts after the first two and lets the stamps carry it); F7 in one line as field observation (work is fragmented, interrupted work is often picked up only after other things come in between); refute misconception 3 with F8, caveated as one experiment; the flip to the asker (F11) is the turn: nobody is careless, the cost of now simply lands on someone else; say once that the real sizes vary (F18); end on the pause_predict

sections.title: Same questions, different timing
sections.goal: the viewer can use two or three team habits that keep every question but change when the non-urgent ones land: batch them, agree focus time with an urgent route, and leave a ready-to-resume note
concepts: agreed focus time and an urgent route
sections.carrier: the same morning layout returns: the non-urgent questions slide into one agreed slot, an urgent route stays open at the edge, and the hidden pile shrinks to one switch; each habit pins to the layout as one short label, tied to the hidden unit it removes
sections.teaching_notes: the reveal of the pause_predict opens this section; refute misconception 4 first (questions are good, F17); each habit gets ONE line plus the unit it removes: batching your own questions (F16) and answering at agreed times (F13, F15), focus time with an urgent route (F12, F15, honestly: in one team's trial it helped and faded when the trial ended, so it needs upkeep), and the ready-to-resume note when you must switch (F14) which shrinks finding your place; F10 supports why a natural break is a better moment; habits are common practice supported in direction, never 'proven'; end by returning to the hook's morning, handled differently

arc.payoff: back to the opening morning: the same questions arrive, held for one agreed slot, and by lunch the plan has moved; the viewer leaves with one question to hold and one habit to propose

practice_ladder.what: one question traced completely: visible minute, then switch, finding your place, attention left behind, each put on the ledger and named

the rest of the morning: the narrator names the parts for the first questions only and the viewer reads the remaining stamps; then the pause_predict asks the viewer to predict the effect of batching before it is shown
the viewer picks the next non-urgent question they were about to send and holds it for a batch, and picks one habit to propose to their team

slowdown_at: the hidden part: switching away and getting back in (sec1)

recall_moments.prompt_sketch: Keep the two columns in mind: visible and hidden. Watch which one grows.
Say the same questions all arrived together, at one agreed time. Which column shrinks: the visible one, or the hidden one? Pause and decide.
recall_moments.answer: the hidden one: the answers still take the same minutes, but there is one switch and one return instead of one for every question
recall_moments.tempting_wrong: the visible one, because it feels like fewer interruptions means less answering; the answering is the same, only the switching is saved

recall_moments.prompt_sketch: Each habit shrinks the hidden column, never the visible one: the questions still get answered.

transfer_tasks: the next time you are about to send a quick question, ask whether it needs an answer now; if not, add it to one message for an agreed time
at your next team meeting, propose one habit: an agreed answer time for non-urgent messages, a focus block with an urgent route, or a ready-to-resume note before switching

persona.voice: a capable colleague who has been both the interrupter and the interrupted; level, a little dry, never preachy
persona.delivery_notes: plain and quick on the hook; slower and lower on the hidden part in sec1; brisker through the morning in sec2 as the stamps speed up; a real stop on the pause; warm and matter-of-fact on the habits, one line each

gagne.attention: hook: the quick question and the untouched plan
gagne.objective: promise: where the cost goes, and habits that stop paying it
gagne.recall_prior: sec1 opens from the familiar morning of small messages
gagne.present: sections in dependency order: one question, then a morning, then timing
gagne.guidance: signature move and the fully traced single question in sec1
gagne.practice: faded morning in sec2 and the pause_predict after it
gagne.feedback: the reveal explains why the hidden column shrinks and why the visible one does not
gagne.assess: pause_predict after sec2; the closing recall_prompt
gagne.transfer: payoff returns to the opening morning; two transfer tasks

merrill.problem_centered: the one morning and the untouched plan run through all three sections
merrill.activation: sec1 bridges from the viewer's own morning of small messages
merrill.demonstration: sec1 shows one question's full cost on the ledger before naming it
merrill.application: sec2 has the viewer read the morning's stamps and predict the batching effect
merrill.integration: transfer tasks: hold the next question; propose one habit to the team

mayer.coherence: one worker, one piece of work, one morning; no second scenario, no statistics, self-interruption (F9) left out
mayer.signalling: one slowdown, on the hidden part
mayer.redundancy: screen shows the ledger, units and short labels; narration explains
mayer.contiguity: each unit stamps as its part is spoken
mayer.segmenting: three short sections, one idea each
mayer.pre_training: sec1 names the three parts on one question before sec2 runs a whole morning

arcs.attention: the scenario hook and the pile that grows
arcs.relevance: their own mornings, and not wanting to be the colleague who never answers
arcs.confidence: a fully traced single question before any prediction
arcs.satisfaction: the opening morning handled differently, with the plan moved by lunch
